claims.text: Adding one additional principal element while maintaining the phosphorus level increases the alloy's compositional complexity.
Adding one additional principal element improves glass-forming ability relative to an otherwise comparable alloy with fewer principal elements.
Adding one additional principal element improves the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
An additional element with sufficient atomic-size contrast and favorable mixing enthalpy will enhance atomic-level disorder.
The intervention is beneficial only when the added element does not promote phase separation or unwanted crystalline phases.
The intervention should work under melt-quenching or similar processing conditions that support amorphization.
An element that acts as a crystallization nucleation site will prevent the proposed benefit.
Greater compositional complexity increases atomic disorder in the modified phosphorus-containing alloy.
Greater compositional complexity broadens the distribution of local chemical environments.
The increased disorder and broader local-environment distribution raise kinetic and thermodynamic barriers to crystallization.
Adding the extra principal element boosts configurational entropy.
Adding the extra principal element accentuates atomic-size mismatch.
The resulting high-entropy state kinetically stabilizes the glass by hindering crystal nucleation and growth.
The intervention extends the supercooled-liquid temperature region.
The modified alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will have a wider supercooled-liquid region than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will have a greater critical casting thickness than the baseline alloy.
The benefit may be absent or detrimental when the added element provides little size or bonding contrast or induces segregation or secondary phases.
